'''Charles F. "Chuck" Stevens''' (September 1, 1934 – October 21, 2022)<ref>[https://www.the-scientist.com/news-opinion/famed-neuroscientist-charles-stevens-dies-at-88-70738 Famed Neuroscientist Charles Stevens Dies at 88]</ref> was an American [[neurobiologist]] at the [[Salk Institute]] in La Jolla.
He was the Vincent J. Coates Professor at the [[Salk Institute for Biological Studies]] and adjunct professor of pharmacology and neuroscience at [[UCSD]]'s School of Medicine. He was also an external professor and member of the science board at the [[Santa Fe Institute]]<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.santafe.edu/about/people/profile/Charles%20Stevens|title = Charles Stevens &#124; Santa Fe Institute}}</ref> and a general member of the [[Aspen Center for Physics]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.aspenphys.org/documents/acp/members.html |title=ACP General Members |access-date=2010-02-10 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100428000140/http://www.aspenphys.org/documents/acp/members.html |archive-date=2010-04-28 }}</ref>

==Major contributions==
He made several seminal discoveries regarding the molecular basis of synaptic transmission.{{Citation needed|date=February 2011}} In 2002, together with [[Dmitri Chklovskii]], Stevens described the "3/5 Power Scaling law of neural circuits."

Stevens and Anderson used noise analysis to infer the conductance of single acetylcholine ion channels. This work paved the way for Nobel laureate [[Erwin Neher]]'s patch clamping techniques. Neher was a postdoctoral associate with Stevens at the [[University of Washington]] and then [[Yale University]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://thorpinstitute.com/html/P-nobel_prize |title=Nobel Prize - the foundation of Electro Acuscope and Myopulse |access-date=2010-02-10 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080724103149/http://thorpinstitute.com/html/P-nobel_prize |archive-date=2008-07-24 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

==Education==
Stevens has a B.A. in psychology from [[Harvard University]], where he began his education hoping to be a physician.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.hhmi.org/bulletin/pdf/dec2003/Dual.pdf |title=Archived copy |access-date=2014-01-07 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061012214547/http://www.hhmi.org/bulletin/pdf/dec2003/Dual.pdf |archive-date=2006-10-12 }}</ref> He then received an M.D. degree at [[Yale University]], and a Ph.D. in biophysics from [[Rockefeller University]] with [[Haldan Keffer Hartline]]. He was a member of the faculties at the [[University of Washington]] Medical School and at [[Yale Medical School]] before joining the Salk Institute.

Stevens was elected member to the [[United States National Academy of Sciences|National Academy of Sciences]] in 1982, and he was formerly an investigator of the [[Howard Hughes Medical Institute]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.hhmi.org/research/investigators/stevens_bio.html|title = Charles F. Stevens}}</ref> He was elected a Fellow of the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] in 1984.<ref name=AAAS>{{cite web|title=Book of Members, 1780-2010: Chapter S|url=http://www.amacad.org/publications/BookofMembers/ChapterS.pdf|publisher=American Academy of Arts and Sciences|access-date=7 April 2011}}</ref> In 2000 he was awarded the [[NAS Award for Scientific Reviewing]] from the [[United States National Academy of Sciences|National Academy of Sciences]].<ref name=Reviewing>{{cite web|title=NAS Award for Scientific Reviewing|url=http://www.nasonline.org/site/PageServer?pagename=AWARDS_scirev|publisher=National Academy of Sciences|access-date=27 February 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110318130922/http://www.nasonline.org/site/PageServer?pagename=AWARDS_scirev|archive-date=2011-03-18|url-status=dead}}</ref>
